parts.partTitle: Reading GC Logs Like a Pro

beats.headline: Why are you still guessing with JVM flags?
beats.subline: Stop copying legacy blog posts. Start reading the ground truth in your GC logs.
beats.narration: Most teams do more harm than good by copying random JVM flags. If you have latency spikes or OOM kills, stop guessing. Start by reading the actual GC logs to see what the collector is doing.

beats.title: Production Logging Config

lines.text: # gc*: Tracks heap transitions & humongous allocs

beats.narration: Use the Unified Logging flag. This config captures everything from evacuation phases to safepoint delays, while capping disk usage at 500MB so you never fill your container storage.

beats.title: Decoding the GC Log Line
beats.code:
GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) 1842M->412M(4096M) 6.412ms
[info][gc,cpu] GC(42) User=0.05s Sys=0.00s Real=0.01s
[info][safepoint] Reaching: 0.18ms, At: 6.51ms

steps.explanation: 1842MB before, 412MB after. If this trend is rising, you have a leak.
If Real time exceeds User time, your container is likely CPU throttled.
High 'Reaching' time means one thread is stalling the entire JVM.

beats.narration: Look for the heap drop. If the baseline trends upward, you have a leak. If Real time is higher than User time, Kubernetes is throttling your CPU. And always check the Reaching safepoint time.

beats.title: GC Log Red Flags

nodes.label: Rising Baseline
nodes.detail: Sawtooth trend climbing after every GC

nodes.label: To-space Exhausted
nodes.detail: G1 ran out of space, forced Full GC

beats.narration: Watch for these three killers. Humongous allocations fragment the heap, while To-space exhausted triggers a stop-the-world Full GC that can freeze your app for seconds.

beats.narration: That is the diagnostic foundation. In Part 2, we compare the collectors and learn why Generational ZGC isn't always the right answer.

beats.headline: Generational ZGC is fast, but is it free?
beats.subline: Sub-millisecond pauses come with a hidden tax on your CPU and memory.
beats.narration: Generational ZGC gives sub-millisecond pauses, but it is not a magic bullet. It requires extra CPU and memory headroom that might actually hurt small microservices.

G1GC is the king of balance for most web services. Switch to Generational ZGC only if you have huge heaps and absolutely require sub-millisecond latency. Otherwise, the load-barrier overhead will cost you.

beats.title: Sizing Memory for Containers

steps.explanation: Leave 30% for Metaspace, JIT cache, and off-heap memory.
If your total RSS exceeds the K8s limit, the kernel kills you instantly.

beats.narration: Never set MaxRAMPercentage to 100. The JVM needs room for Metaspace, thread stacks, and JIT code. If your total process memory hits the container limit, the kernel sends a SIGKILL, and you get Exit Code 137.

beats.title: The Collector Trade-off
beats.narration: Pick your tool for the job. Parallel for batch, G1 for services, ZGC for massive scale. Don't over-engineer until you have the metrics to justify the complexity.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: G1GC is the default for a reason

beats.headline: Your memory leak is hiding in a ThreadLocal.
beats.subline: Pooled threads + request context = a recipe for disaster.
beats.narration: Memory leaks in Java happen when objects stay reachable from a GC root. The most common culprit? Forgetting to clear a ThreadLocal in a pooled servlet thread.

beats.title: The ThreadLocal Trap

steps.explanation: Without clear(), the object stays in the thread's map forever.
Always clear in a finally block to prevent leaks on worker threads.

beats.narration: Servlet containers reuse threads. If you store data in a ThreadLocal and don't clear it, that object stays pinned in memory for the life of the thread. Always use a finally block.

beats.title: Capturing the Dump
beats.narration: Configure your JVM to dump on OOM so you have the evidence. If you need a manual dump, use jcmd, but remember it pauses the JVM, so drain your traffic first.

beats.title: MAT Forensics Workflow

nodes.label: Shallow vs Retained
nodes.detail: Shallow is small, Retained is massive

nodes.label: Path to GC Roots
nodes.detail: Find the static field pinning the data

beats.narration: Open the dump in Eclipse MAT. Look at the Dominator Tree, compare shallow versus retained heap, and trace the path to GC roots to find the static field holding the reference.

beats.headline: Stop tuning and start measuring.
beats.subline: Performance isn't about flags; it's about the bottleneck you haven't found yet.
beats.narration: Before you change a single flag, you must prove the bottleneck. Most performance issues are application code, not the JVM. JFR is your best friend here.

beats.title: Production Profiling with JFR

lines.text: jcmd <PID> JFR.start name=baseline settings=profile duration=120s filename=/tmp/base.jfr

beats.narration: JFR has negligible overhead. Capture a baseline under load, then open it in Mission Control. Check for lock contention and I/O wait times before blaming the garbage collector.

beats.title: The Tuning Workflow

nodes.label: Tweak GC
nodes.detail: Change one flag at a time

beats.narration: Follow this loop. Measure, optimize your code to reduce allocations, and only then tweak the GC. Never change more than one flag at a time, or you will never know what worked.

bottom.label: Senior Workflow
bottom.code:
1. Measure
2. Fix Allocations
3. One Flag Change

beats.narration: Avoid the chaos. Document every flag you add. If you can't explain why a flag is there, remove it. Your future self will thank you when you upgrade to the next Java LTS.
